title: Sense organs
summary: How do the eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin detect stimuli?
cards.0.p: Light, sound, pressure or an odor molecule is a stimulus. A receptor picks up the stimulus and turns its energy into an electrical impulse. A sensory neuron then carries this impulse to the right sensory center in the brain.
cards.0.svg#3: turns the stimulus into an impulse
cards.0.svg#5: carries the impulse to the brain
cards.0.svg#8: e.g. light → retina → optic nerve → brain
cards.0.key: If a stimulus is below the threshold, no impulse forms. That is why you do not feel a very light touch.
cards.1.p: Receptors are grouped by the stimulus they detect. Mechanoreceptors detect touch and sound, thermoreceptors detect temperature, chemoreceptors detect taste and smell, and photoreceptors detect light. When the response to a lasting stimulus fades, this is called adaptation.
cards.1.svg#18: Adaptation: the stimulus lasts but the response fades
cards.1.svg#19: e.g. after a while you stop feeling the watch on your wrist
cards.1.key: Pain receptors adapt very little, because pain is a warning signal. Balance is also detected by mechanoreceptors.
cards.1.once.soru: You notice a smell when you enter a room. Why can't you smell it a few minutes later?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: As the same stimulus continues, the receptor's response fades.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: The odor molecules are still in the room. Someone who just walked in notices the smell right away.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The nose is clear. What changes is the receptor's response.
cards.2.p: The eye has three layers. The outer sclera becomes the clear cornea at the front. The middle choroid forms the iris at the front. The inner retina holds the receptors.
cards.2.key: The opening in the middle of the iris is called the pupil. The space between the cornea and the lens is filled with aqueous humor, and the space behind the lens with vitreous humor. The cornea has no blood vessels.
cards.2.etk.soru: Tap the parts of the eye and think about the path light takes.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.0.acik: The cornea is the clear front part of the sclera. It is the first structure to bend light.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.1.acik: The iris is the colored front part of the choroid. Its muscles narrow and widen the pupil.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.2.acik: The pupil is the opening in the middle of the iris. It controls how much light enters the eye.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.3.acik: The lens is flexible and clear. It focuses light onto the retina by changing its thickness.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.4.acik: The sclera is the tough outermost layer. It protects the eye and gives it its shape.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.5.acik: The retina is the innermost layer. Its rod and cone cells turn light into impulses.
cards.2.etk.noktalar.6.acik: The optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain. Where the nerve leaves, there are no receptors. This is the blind spot.
cards.3.p: Eyebrows catch sweat, and eyelashes catch dust. The eyelids wipe the eye. The lacrimal gland keeps the eye moist, and the enzyme lysozyme in tears breaks down bacteria.
cards.3.key: The lacrimal gland sits at the upper outer corner of the eye.
cards.3.once.soru: Why does your nose run when you cry?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: Extra tears drain into the nasal cavity through a duct at the inner corner of the eye.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The fluid running from the nose is mostly tears.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Breathing rate does not make the nose run.
cards.4.p: The lens is flexible, and its thickness is set by the ciliary muscles and the suspensory ligaments. When you look at something near, the lens gets thicker. When you look far away, it gets thinner. This is called accommodation.
cards.4.key: When you look at something near, the muscle contracts and the ligaments loosen. With age, the lens loses its flexibility and seeing near things gets harder. This is called presbyopia.
cards.5.p: Rod cells in the retina are sensitive to dim light, but they do not tell colors apart. Cone cells detect colors and detail in bright light. There are three types of cones: red, green and blue.
cards.5.key: The pigment rhodopsin in rods is made with vitamin A. That is why a lack of vitamin A causes night blindness.
cards.5.once.soru: In moonlight you can see your surroundings, but you can hardly tell colors apart. Why?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: In dim light, cones are not stimulated enough. Rods do not tell colors apart.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: In dim light the pupil gets bigger.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The thickness of the lens affects focus, not color.
cards.6.h: The image, the fovea and the blind spot
cards.6.p: Light passes through the cornea, the pupil, the lens and the vitreous humor, in that order. An upside-down, smaller image forms on the retina. The sharpest image forms at the fovea, and no image forms at the blind spot.
cards.6.svg#1: on the retina: inverted, smaller, real
cards.6.svg#5: the brain perceives the image upright
cards.6.key: Cones are packed densely in the fovea. The optic nerve leaves at the blind spot, and there are no receptors there.
cards.6.once.soru: The image on your retina is upside down. So why do you see the world upright?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Perception happens in the brain, and the brain interprets the image as upright.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: The lens does not fix the image. It makes it upside down.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The image on the retina really is upside down.
cards.7.p: In nearsightedness (myopia), the focus falls in front of the retina and faraway objects look blurry. A concave lens corrects it. In farsightedness (hyperopia), the focus falls behind the retina and nearby objects look blurry. A convex lens corrects it.
cards.7.svg#4: focus in front of the retina
cards.7.key: In a nearsighted eye the eyeball is long, and in a farsighted eye it is short. Lens strength is measured in diopters. −2 D is a diverging lens with a focal length of 50 cm.
cards.8.p: In astigmatism, the curve of the cornea is uneven, and a cylindrical lens is used. In a cataract, the lens becomes cloudy. In color blindness, a defect in the cones usually makes red and green hard to tell apart.
cards.8.key: For a cataract, an artificial lens is put in with surgery. Red-green color blindness is an X-linked recessive trait and is more common in males.
cards.8.once.soru: Color blindness comes from a defect in which retinal cells?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Three types of cones tell colors apart. If one of them is defective, some colors get mixed up.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Rods do not tell colors apart anyway.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Even with a healthy optic nerve, a defect in the cones causes color blindness.
cards.9.p: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. The hammer, anvil and stirrup bones amplify this vibration and pass it through the oval window to the cochlea. The organ of Corti in the cochlea turns the vibration into an impulse.
cards.9.key: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat. When your ears pop as you swallow on a plane, this tube is balancing the pressure.
cards.9.etk.soru: Tap the parts of the ear and follow the path of sound.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.0.acik: The ear canal carries sound to the eardrum. Its hairs and earwax trap dust.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.1.acik: The eardrum is a thin membrane that vibrates with sound waves. It separates the outer ear from the middle ear.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.2.acik: These ossicles are the smallest bones in the body. They amplify the eardrum's vibration and pass it to the inner ear.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.3.acik: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat. It balances the pressure on both sides of the eardrum.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.4.acik: The semicircular canals are three canals at right angles to each other. The fluid inside them lets us sense the head turning.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.5.acik: The hair cells of the organ of Corti inside the cochlea turn vibrations into impulses.
cards.9.etk.noktalar.6.acik: The auditory nerve carries impulses from the cochlea to the hearing center in the brain.
cards.10.p: The part of the cochlea near the entrance vibrates with high-pitched sounds, and the tip vibrates with low-pitched sounds. This is how the brain tells the pitch of a sound. As a sound gets louder, more hair cells are stimulated.
cards.10.svg#15: long exposure above 85 dB damages hair cells
cards.10.key: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). With age, the ability to hear high-pitched sounds fades first.
cards.10.once.soru: A dog hears a dog whistle, but you don't. Why?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The human ear hears sounds between about 20 and 20,000 Hz. The whistle's sound is above this range.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: The whistle's sound is strong. The issue is its frequency.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.yazi: Sound does not travel in air
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Since the dog hears it, the sound must be traveling through the air.
cards.11.p: Balance is sensed in the inner ear. When the head turns, the fluid in the three semicircular canals moves. The ear stones in the utricle and saccule let us sense tilting and acceleration.
cards.11.key: Balance information goes to the cerebellum through the vestibular nerve. In motion sickness, the inner ear senses movement, but the eyes see the still inside of the vehicle. This mismatch causes nausea.
cards.12.p: Smell and taste are detected by chemoreceptors. Odor molecules dissolve in the mucus of the olfactory epithelium in the nose. The taste buds on the tongue are stimulated by substances dissolved in saliva.
cards.12.key: The "tongue map" is a myth. Every part of the tongue can detect all five tastes.
cards.12.once.soru: Why can't you taste food well when you have a cold?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: A blocked nose cannot pick up smells, and much of what we call taste comes from smell.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: A cold does not kill taste buds.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: The problem is in the nose, not the tongue.
cards.13.p: The skin is made of the epidermis, the dermis and a fat layer. The Malpighian layer of the epidermis divides and makes the pigment melanin. The dermis holds glands and receptors for touch, pressure, temperature and pain.
cards.13.key: Meissner corpuscles detect touch, and Pacinian corpuscles detect pressure. Textbooks often link Ruffini endings to heat and Krause bulbs to cold. Current research shows that temperature is mainly detected by free nerve endings.
cards.13.once.soru: Why does your skin get darker the longer you stay in the sun?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: The Malpighian layer makes more melanin to protect against UV rays.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Redness comes from blood flow. Lasting darkening comes from melanin.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Skin color comes from the pigment melanin, not from dead cells.
cards.14.p: When the hair cells of the organ of Corti die, they are not replaced. So loud noise can cause permanent hearing loss. Smell and taste cells, on the other hand, are renewed. Protect your eyes from UV rays and your skin from the sun.
cards.14.svg#1: Take breaks from screens and look into the distance.
cards.14.svg#4: Avoid long exposure to loud noise.
cards.14.svg#5: Don't put sharp objects in your ears.
cards.14.svg#7: Use sunscreen and avoid the midday sun.
cards.14.svg#11: Take care of your mouth and teeth.
cards.14.key: If the people next to you can hear the music from your headphones, it is too loud. You should also have your eyes checked regularly.
cards.14.once.soru: Are hair cells killed by loud noise replaced by new ones?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The hair cells of the organ of Corti are not renewed, so the loss is permanent.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: Smell and taste cells are renewed, but hair cells are not.
cards.15.p:
• A receptor picks up the stimulus, a sensory neuron carries it to the brain, and perception happens in the brain.
• Rods work in dim light and cones handle color. The sharpest image forms at the fovea.
• Myopia is corrected with a concave lens and hyperopia with a convex lens.
• The cochlea handles hearing, and the semicircular canals handle balance.
• Smell and taste are detected by chemoreceptors.
cards.15.svg#18: perception always happens in the brain
quiz.0.q: Put in order the path a sound takes from the ear to the brain.
quiz.0.ogeler.3: Organ of Corti in the cochlea
quiz.0.e: Sound travels down the ear canal and makes the eardrum vibrate. The ossicles amplify the vibration and pass it to the inner ear. The hair cells of the organ of Corti turn the vibration into an impulse, and the auditory nerve carries the impulse to the brain. Perception happens in the brain.
quiz.1.q: Match each situation with the structure that detects it.
quiz.1.e: Rotation is detected by the semicircular canals, and linear acceleration by the ear stones in the utricle and saccule. Smell and taste are detected by chemoreceptors, and temperature by thermoreceptors in the skin.
quiz.2.q: Put each feature under the photoreceptor it belongs to.
quiz.2.e: Rods work in dim light and allow night vision, but they do not tell colors apart. Cones detect colors and detail in bright light. They come in three types, for red, green and blue, and are dense in the fovea.
quiz.3.q: Someone reading a book looks up through the window at a faraway tree. What changes in their eye?
quiz.3.o.0: Ciliary muscles contract, ligaments loosen, the lens thickens.
quiz.3.o.1: Ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tighten, the lens thins.
quiz.3.o.2: The iris contracts and thins the lens.
quiz.3.o.3: The ligaments loosen and the lens thins.
quiz.3.e: When looking far, the ciliary muscles relax and the suspensory ligaments tighten and pull on the lens. So the lens gets thinner and bends light less.
quiz.3.y.0: This happens when looking at something near. When you look far, the muscles relax and the lens gets thinner.
quiz.3.y.2: The iris only adjusts the pupil. The thickness of the lens is changed by the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments.
quiz.3.y.3: A loose ligament cannot pull on the lens. The lens gets thinner only when the ligaments tighten.
A:ozet: Watch a stimulus become a perception. Adjust the pupil to light, focus the lens on something near, choose glasses for a nearsighted eye and follow the path of sound in the ear.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Imagine someone whose eyes and optic nerves are healthy, but whose visual center in the brain is damaged. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The eye turns light into impulses, but it is the brain that interprets the impulses and turns them into an image.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Colors are told apart by the cones in the retina. When the visual center is damaged, no image is perceived at all.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Perception happens in the center in the brain, not in the receptor. So brain damage can make even a healthy eye blind.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The iris uses its muscles to set the size of the pupil. Change the light and make the pupil as wide as it can get.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: In dim light the pupil gets bigger and more light reaches the retina.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: In dim light the pupil got bigger, and in bright light it gets smaller. This is a reflex, and it protects the retina from too much light.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The suspensory ligaments attach the lens to the ciliary body. Use the switch to look near and watch the muscle, the ligaments and the lens.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: How does the lens get thicker when you look at something near?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: When the ligaments loosen, the flexible lens thickens on its own and bends light more. This focuses the light from a nearby object onto the retina.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: This happens when looking far. The tight ligaments pull on the lens and make it thinner.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The iris only sets the size of the pupil. The shape of the lens is changed by the ciliary muscles.
A:adimlar.3.metin: In a nearsighted eye the eyeball is long. Light from a faraway object focuses in front of the retina and the image is blurry. Pick a lens and move the focus onto the retina.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: The focus falls too far forward. A minus lens that spreads the light a little pushes the focus back.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: The concave (diverging) lens spread the light and the focus landed on the retina. Nearsighted people see far things blurry and wear minus lenses.
A:adimlar.4.metin: In a farsighted eye the eyeball is short and the focus falls behind the retina. This person sees near things blurry. Try the lenses.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: This lens spreads light and pushes the focus even further back. It corrects nearsightedness but makes farsightedness worse.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A converging lens gathers the light early and pulls the focus forward onto the retina. Farsighted people wear plus lenses.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A cylindrical lens corrects an uneven curve of the cornea, which is astigmatism. It does not move the focus forward.
A:adimlar.5.metin: A patient's eardrum and cochlea are healthy, but the ossicles in the middle ear have hardened and cannot move. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Where does the sound get stuck in this ear?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The eardrum is healthy, so it vibrates. The problem is in the ossicles that should carry the vibration.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A stirrup that cannot move cannot vibrate the oval window. Even though the cochlea and nerve are healthy, the signal never reaches the inner ear. This is called conductive hearing loss.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The nerve is healthy, but since the cochlea is not stimulated, no impulse forms for it to carry.
A:adimlar.6.metin: You just got off a Ferris wheel, and even though you are standing still, your head is spinning. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Why is your head spinning even though you have stopped?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The cochlea is for hearing. It detects sound vibrations, not rotation.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The Eustachian tube only balances the pressure on both sides of the eardrum. It does not detect rotation.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: The canal fluid is still moving
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The canal stops with you, but the fluid inside keeps flowing for a while because of inertia. The hair cells still tell the cerebellum you are turning, while your eyes show you have stopped.
A:kapanis.0: A receptor turns a stimulus into an impulse, and perception happens in the brain.
A:kapanis.1: The pupil gets bigger in dim light and smaller in bright light. When looking near, the ciliary muscle contracts and the lens gets thicker.
A:kapanis.2: In myopia the focus is in front of the retina and a concave lens is needed. In hyperopia the focus is behind the retina and a convex lens is needed.
A:kapanis.3: Sound travels from the eardrum through the hammer, anvil and stirrup to the cochlea. The semicircular canals detect rotation, and the utricle and saccule detect tilting.
A:kapanis.4: In dim light the rods work and colors are not seen. Cones tell colors apart in bright light.
